# Daniel Arcé
Daniel Arcé works across interaction design and front-end development, using working software to explore how people find information and act on it.

## About
Hello, I’m Daniel Arcé.

I’m a product designer and design technologist in Toronto, with a hands-on front-end development practice. I use working software to explore how people find information and act on it. That interest connects my work in media and enterprise software with the independent products I design and build today.

### Designing through working software

A working prototype gives a team something to try. A selection leads to another view; that view may expose a choice that was easy to miss in a static screen. Trying the interaction helps us decide what to keep, what to change, and what the implementation needs to support.

I stay involved as those decisions reach production. My front-end work includes React and TypeScript, with accessibility built into the behaviour of the interface. Keyboard interaction and focus management are part of making that behaviour work for the people using it.

### Carrying an idea into production

At [MSNBC](/projects/msnbc/), I helped take a dedicated video experience from product definition through working prototypes to launch in six months. I proposed collapsible panels so viewers could browse coverage and read comments while the video continued playing. Those panels became working front-end interactions, developed with the internal team and external vendors.

At [PhotoShelter](/projects/photoshelter/), my work combined product R&D with accessibility engineering. A workflow-automation prototype exposed integration issues before production development and informed Smart Galleries. Alongside that R&D work, I led a WCAG audit and front-end remediation, including keyboard support across Web Components, and helped other developers adopt accessible patterns.

### Exploring and describing images

My independent image products pursue two related interests: visual exploration and image description.

**Visual exploration** is the focus of [Visual Search Workbench](/projects/visual-search-workbench/), a macOS app I designed and released. A person can start with words or a picture, then follow similar images without tagging the collection first. A map offers another way to browse those relationships. I wanted to leave room for a useful picture to suggest a direction the original query did not anticipate, while keeping processing on the Mac. I have tested the app on an 8 GB machine.

**Image description** is the focus of [AltContext](/projects/altcontext/), which is still in development. It combines a photograph with a publisher’s named people roster and the page’s context to draft a description in WordPress. The editor reviews the identity and wording before applying the text. The intended benefit is more useful context for blind readers, including who is pictured when that matters to the page.

### Keeping design decisions available during development

AI-assisted development introduced another problem into my practice: decisions and review findings could be lost between coding sessions. I built [WorkBay](/projects/workbay/) to preserve those records outside the conversation and make them available to a later session, including when I move to another supported coding tool. Its orchestration layer lets me deploy different agents across the orchestration, implementation, and review stages. In my use, varying the agent composition across those stages makes the agents check each other’s work and helps soften the swings in inference speed and quality that can follow a model release.

Design reviews produce records worth keeping too. I use UX maps to inventory existing interfaces and examine proposed changes. Those maps can be rendered as text screens and flows for people and AI tools to review. [Heuristics Canon](/research/heuristics-canon/), a collection I maintain, supplies specific questions and references for the critique. The resulting findings guide changes that I check in the running interface.

### Get in touch

I’m interested in senior and lead product design roles where I can contribute to exploration and stay involved through delivery.

[Email me](mailto:daniel.arce@gmail.com) about a role or a project.

Portrait by Liam Maloney</a>.

## Projects

### Visual Search Workbench
*Find a picture, then follow its visual neighbours*
Year: 2026
Tags: Product Design, Interaction Design, Visual Search, UMAP, SwiftUI, Core ML
Summary: Search your photo folders by words or an example image, then explore related pictures on a UMAP map. Processing stays on the Mac.

Visual Search Workbench lets you find photographs in your own folders and explore where they lead. Start with words or a reference picture, inspect the results, then make a promising image the next search. A similarity map offers another route through the collection, without requiring you to tag the photographs first.

I designed and built the app to explore this movement between finding a picture and developing a visual direction. The app runs on Apple Silicon Macs, keeps image processing on-device, and has been tested on an 8 GB machine.

![A search for flowers returns photographs from a film-scan collection, with a selected image open for inspection.](/images/work/sis-search-layer.png)

*These application captures show version 0.2.0, under the earlier name Semantic Image Search. The downloadable release documented here is 0.2.3.*

## Give the search a starting point

The search begins with the folders you choose. The app reads their photographs into a separate search index and leaves the originals where they are. That index lets you search by what a picture depicts even when its filename is a camera number.

You can give the search two kinds of query: a description or a reference picture. A description is useful when you remember a subject but not the filename. A reference picture is useful when showing what interests you is easier than putting it into words.

Drop a reference picture into the app, or choose **Find similar** on a photograph in the collection. That photograph becomes the query for the next set of results. A banner names the reference, and **Back to text results** returns to the earlier query.

![A flower photograph is named as the reference for Find similar, above the resulting images.](/images/work/sis-similarity-search.png)

A result can therefore become a new direction. You might begin by looking for flowers and continue because a particular image suggests something useful for a colour study. That is the kind of exploration I wanted the app to support.

## Explore the collection on a map

The **Similarity** view arranges related images on a map using UMAP. UMAP takes the images’ numerical representations and looks for a layout that keeps neighbours near one another. The result gives you regions to explore instead of a list to read from top to bottom.

A region becomes useful when you can see the photographs behind it. Select a region, and its pictures appear in the linked grid. The grid lets you judge the images themselves and choose another one to follow.

![A Similarity map of a 2,314-photo collection, with photographs from a selected region shown in the grid.](/images/work/sis-layers-umap.png)

*Selecting a region connects the overview to the photographs it contains.*

The map suggests where to look. Its groups are not automatically named categories, and the gaps between them are not exact measures of visual difference. [Finding a Visual Direction with UMAP](/research/visual-search-workbench-process/) explains the method and the design idea; the [interaction reference](/research/visual-search-workbench-screen-reference/) follows the controls and views.

## Look at the selection by place or time

A selection can be explored through **Similarity**, **Places**, or **Timeline**. Similarity organises the images by relationships in their representations. Places uses recorded coordinates. Timeline uses dates to show broader or narrower periods.

The selection carries between those views, and each view retains its zoom and pan when you change tabs. You can examine the same material from another angle without rebuilding the view. Selecting an individual photograph opens its available file metadata, including camera information, capture time, and location.

## Take a cutout into another project

A useful photograph may contain a subject you want to use in a composition. The app’s experimental cutout feature proposes subject layers with transparent backgrounds. Those layers can be inspected and saved for use elsewhere.

![A cat photograph with proposed cutout layers, each marked experimental.](/images/work/sis-cat-layers-detail.png)

The layers still require judgment: an edge can be rough, a label can be wrong, or the proposed separation may not suit the composition. Cutouts remain a secondary experiment alongside search and exploration.

## Keep the work on the Mac

The app bundles the search and cutout models, so they are available without a first-launch model download. The models process the photographs locally. My network checks found no gallery data leaving the device in the tested flows.

The 8 GB test establishes a working configuration rather than a memory requirement for every library. Larger collections still need measurement, and an outside-user study has not yet run. That study needs to examine both finding a remembered image and discovering useful material for a creative brief.

## Download

[Download Visual Search Workbench 0.2.3](https://dl.darce.xyz/) for Apple Silicon, macOS 14 or later. Choose `VisualSearchWorkbench-0.2.3.dmg`, approximately 295 MB.

The app is not notarized by Apple, so macOS may block its first launch. The release instructions explain the **Privacy & Security → Open Anyway** option. The [GitHub release repository](https://github.com/darce/visual-search-workbench) provides the built app, model-licence information, and a `SHA256SUMS` file. It does not publish the application source.

### AltContext
*Use the photograph, confirmed identities, and page context to draft image descriptions*
Year: 2026
Tags: Product Design, Human-AI Interaction, Accessibility, React, TypeScript, WordPress, Python
Summary: AltContext combines a photograph with a publisher’s named people roster and page context. Editors review the proposed identity and wording before applying the text in WordPress.

A description such as “a person singing on a stage” can explain an activity while leaving out who is pictured. When the page concerns a particular performer, that identity may be part of the photograph’s meaning.

AltContext is a WordPress product I am designing and building to bring that context into image descriptions. It combines the photograph with identities from a publisher’s named people roster and information from the page. The editor reviews the proposed identity and wording before applying the text. The intended benefit is more useful context for blind readers; the product is still in development.

## Build a description from the photograph, the roster, and the page

The description draws on three inputs with different roles: **the photograph**, **the roster**, and **the page**. Keeping those roles distinct helps explain what supports each part of the proposed text.

**The photograph** supplies visual information about the scene. An image model may describe a microphone, clothing, or the setting. Those observations provide material for the description without requiring the model to identify the person from general knowledge.

**The roster** supplies names the site has established. An editor builds the roster in WordPress by associating groups of faces with people and correcting mistaken groupings. Face matching compares a face in a new image with that site-specific reference. A proposed match still needs review, and the naming policy determines whether a name may be used.

**The page** supplies publishing context, including the image caption and surrounding post. That context helps determine which information matters: a performer’s identity may be important in an event report, while a discussion of a garment may call for attention to the clothing. [W3C’s image guidance](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/images/) explains how an image’s purpose and context shape its text alternative.

The page cannot establish everything about the photograph. A name mentioned in an article does not, by itself, prove who is pictured. AltContext’s reconciliation step distinguishes information supported by something in the image from context about the page or event, so background information is not simply repeated as though it were visible.

## Review the proposal before applying it

The proposed identity gives the editor a match to inspect. The editor can compare the image with reference photographs and decide whether the person should be named. That decision informs the draft description, whose wording can then be reviewed or changed before it is applied.

The draft and the applied text remain separate. Generating a description does not itself publish it, and a suggested name need not be accepted. The publishing workflow also supports a longer description alongside alt text. An image marked as decorative can skip generation and use an empty text alternative.

## Try the decisions in a practice copy

The guided walkthrough follows the identity decision through to the resulting text. It starts with saved face-match results from a development run. Confirming a match or keeping a person unnamed changes the practice draft; the draft can then be edited, applied to the practice copy, or restored with undo.

The practice copy does not publish to a live page. Its recognition results are saved rather than generated live. An optional live-description path is a separate operation whose availability depends on the service.

[Open the guided walkthrough](https://demo.altcontext.com/wp-admin/admin.php?page=alt-context-dashboard#/guided-prototype). Access is managed through the [AltContext site](https://altcontext.com).

## Connect the interface to the stored decision

My work covers the interaction design and the implementation behind it. The admin interface uses React and TypeScript, the WordPress integration uses PHP, and the supporting recognition and description services use Python/FastAPI. Working across those parts lets me follow an editorial action from its control on screen to the result that is stored.

I use [WorkBay’s UX-map workflow](/projects/workbay/#review-the-interface-as-well-as-the-code) to inventory the interface and produce screens and flows for review. Review findings guide implementation changes, which I check in the running interface. These reviews address structure and behaviour; evaluation with editors and readers has a different job.

## Make the processing and retention choices explicit

AltContext uses a WordPress host and a hosted processing service. WordPress remains the source of record for names, editorial corrections, and saved descriptions. Recognition and description processing run on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, so images leave the WordPress host for that work. The hosted service stores the recognition representations used to compare faces.

Those hosted records have retention settings, export and purge operations, and controls for withholding names from generated text. Recognition data is retained by default unless another retention mode is selected. Export and purge operations leave an audit trail; purging the recognition data does not remove that trail.

These controls describe the implementation, not a completed legal compliance assessment. They also distinguish AltContext’s hosted processing from on-device processing. Saved descriptions remain in WordPress even when a new service request cannot run.

## Evaluate the description and the review

The evaluation has two audiences: **readers** who use the description and **editors** who review it. Readers need the text to preserve useful context. Editors need to recognise plausible mistakes and correct them before applying the description.

Model comparisons have examined whether supplied identities survive into the text and whether page context introduces unsupported claims. Automated checks cover the plugin and services, including accessibility checks on the admin interface. Those checks address particular behaviours; they do not yet establish the reader benefit or the reliability of editorial correction.

Evaluation with blind readers and editors is therefore still needed. The product’s purpose is to make an image more informative, and those evaluations must establish whether the resulting text achieves that purpose.

### PhotoShelter: Product R&D & Accessibility at Enterprise Scale
*Product R&D and accessibility for a large DAM platform*
Year: 2021
Tags: Product R&D, Prototyping, Accessibility, Interaction Design, Web Components, OpenCV.js, Enterprise SaaS
Summary: R&D prototyping that cut downstream implementation effort by an internal estimate of roughly 30%, and WCAG 2.1 audit and remediation on contracts worth a combined $9.2M ARR that were exposed if compliance could not be demonstrated, across a media platform serving 80,000+ users and 1B+ files.

## R&D prototyping

Working with the Chief Architect, I built exploratory prototypes outside the production timeline to answer product questions cheaply and catch integration problems before they reached production.

### Workflow automation interface

This prototype informed the [Smart Galleries](https://support.photoshelterbrands.com/hc/en-us/articles/10657698741655-Smart-Galleries) feature. Building it outside the production path surfaced integration issues earlier and reduced development effort by an internal estimate of roughly 30%.

### Client-side image blur comparison

Built with OpenCV.js to test whether image analysis could run fully in the browser without backend resources. The prototype showed that lightweight computer-vision workflows were viable in static-file environments, even though it did not ship as a standalone feature.

## Accessibility

PhotoShelter's customer base includes universities and professional sports organizations, and several key contracts worth a combined $9.2M ARR were exposed if the product could not demonstrate [ADA](https://www.ada.gov/law-and-regs/ada/) and WCAG compliance. I led the WCAG 2.1 audit and front-end remediation effort for PhotoShelter's core product to close that gap.

The initial audit surfaced two classes of issues: fast fixes such as missing ARIA attributes and unlabeled controls, and deeper structural problems such as mouse-only navigation across core menus.

### Keyboard navigation for every menu

![Keyboard navigation for main menu](/images/photoshelter-keyboard-navigation.gif)*Keyboard navigation for the main menu*

Before this work, every menu in the product was mouse-only. Keyboard access is essential for users with limited mobility and speeds things up for power users who prefer shortcuts.

The hardest part was keyboard support across Shadow DOM-based components. Because PhotoShelter relied on Polymer and Web Components, focus and keyboard events did not move cleanly across shadow boundaries. I built a custom layer to bridge those boundaries so interactive elements remained reachable and usable without switching interaction modes.

![The main menu goes from mouse to keyboard control](/images/photoshelter-empty-trash.gif)*Mouse to keyboard control, no mode switch needed*

## Team adoption

I mentored four developers on accessibility patterns and introduced review checklists so accessibility was built into new work rather than added later as remediation.

### MSNBC Video: From Product Concept to Launch in Six Months
*Product definition, interaction design, working prototypes, and launch*
Year: 2014
Tags: Product Design, Interaction Design, Prototyping, Front-End, AngularJS, Drupal, Media Platform
Summary: Helped take MSNBC’s dedicated video experience from initial product definition through functional prototypes, interaction design, production development, and an on-schedule launch.

## Context

MSNBC.com had recently been rebuilt on Drupal following the Microsoft/NBC split. [Lullabot’s account](https://www.lullabot.com/articles/msnbc-video-and-drupalcon-case-study) describes the broader site as a ground-up rebuild that launched in October 2013. Once that site was live, the network needed a dedicated video experience.

The new surface had to support watching live and archived coverage while discovering what to watch next. Sending viewers away from the player to browse would break that continuity. The product problem was to make exploration and playback work together on the same page.

My project record describes a hard six-month deadline, with partner-litigation risk if the launch slipped. Working prototypes therefore had to move the team toward a production decision within a fixed delivery window.

## My role

I used functional prototypes to propose how the video experience should behave, then implemented front-end patterns for production. Doing both the design and the implementation meant I could carry a question into working software and refine it with the team.

I collaborated with MSNBC’s internal team, external vendors, and stakeholders as the prototypes evolved. I proposed and implemented interface patterns within that shared process; I did not independently own the entire product direction or the broader MSNBC.com rebuild. My remit covered the dedicated video experience and the AngularJS components I contributed to MSNBC’s in-house CMS, which I integrated with the Drupal backend powering the broader site.

## The video platform

### From concept to working prototypes

The initial concept centred on continuous viewing: a person should be able to watch coverage while looking through related stories and engagement features. I translated that goal into working prototypes, so the conversation could move from a proposed layout to how the interface behaved.

The prototypes went through multiple iterations with stakeholders. I then carried those proposals into production development, so the behaviour the prototypes settled is the behaviour that shipped.

### Collapsible panes around a running player

My proposal was to give the surrounding content its own collapsible panes. The player kept running while a viewer opened the discussion, scanned the latest coverage, or closed both to watch at full width. Choosing what to watch next never required leaving the page or interrupting the stream.

That put playback and conversation on screen at the same time. Comments usually lived below the fold or on a separate page, so a viewer who wanted to read them gave up the video to do it. Here they sat beside the player and could be dismissed. The arrangement is unremarkable on a video site today; in 2013 it was a proposal that needed a working prototype before the team would commit to it.

In live coverage that continuity mattered most, because the broadcast could move on while someone was choosing another story. An “Up next” row below the player brought the next viewing choice close to the current clip, and the adjacent video list provided a broader route through coverage.

The responsive layouts kept the player prominent as the available width changed. Desktop had room for horizontal video rows and a side panel; narrower layouts placed recommendations into vertical lists. The arrangement let browsing adapt to the screen while keeping the current video central.

![MSNBC video interface with a large player, clip details and an Up next row on the left, and a list of latest videos on the right.](/images/msnbc-interface.png)

*Surviving interface capture, from December 2016 rather than launch day. The player, next-video choices, and broader browsing list share the same viewing surface.*

![MSNBC video mockup showing phone, tablet and desktop layouts: the player remains prominent, recommendations stack at narrower widths, and a discussion panel sits beside the desktop player.](/images/msnbc-watch-full-mockup.webp)

*Responsive interface mockup showing the player and surrounding content at different screen widths.*

### Through production to launch

The video platform launched on schedule within the six-month window. According to my project record, meeting that deadline helped avert the partner-litigation risk associated with a delayed launch.

### WorkBay
*Keep coding tasks and review history available across AI sessions*
Year: 2026
Tags: Developer Tooling, AI-Assisted Development, Interaction Design, MCP, Python, SQLite
Summary: WorkBay records tasks, decisions, review findings, and test evidence in the repository. Later sessions can retrieve the record across supported AI coding tools.

WorkBay keeps the state of a coding task outside any one AI conversation. It preserves recorded decisions and unfinished review findings so a later session can resume the work, including when I switch between supported coding tools.

I built WorkBay while developing projects such as [AltContext](/projects/altcontext/). A recap could say that a task was nearly finished while leaving out the finding that still blocked it. I needed the next session to retrieve that finding and its evidence, not infer the remaining work from a general account of progress.

## Keep a record the next session can use

Each repository has a SQLite database at `.task-state/handoff.db`. The database holds the task record: what is active, which decisions have been made, what the reviews found, and which checks were run.

The task identifies the current work. Decisions preserve their rationale, while findings retain their severity and resolution status. Test records preserve the commands and results. Together, those records let a later session examine the parts of the work that matter to its next step.

A session loads a selected context packet from the database. That packet brings recorded history into the current conversation without requiring the whole history to be repeated. Optional semantic retrieval supplies another way to find earlier decisions when the current question uses different words.

The retrieved records remain material to inspect. Similarity can suggest that an earlier fix is relevant; it cannot itself close a finding or authorise a merge.

## Resume in another coding tool

WorkBay exposes the same project record to supported tools, including Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and VS Code Copilot. A session in another tool can retrieve the decisions and findings that the earlier session left behind.

That continuity concerns recorded state. The tools still have different setup requirements and capabilities, and reasoning that was never recorded does not become available simply because the database exists. The record removes one switching cost: reconstructing project history from a conversation held elsewhere.

## Carry a review finding through to a change

An authoring agent can submit work to a reviewing agent without sharing its conversation. The reviewer records findings against the task. Those findings remain available after the review session ends, so the author can retrieve them and address the changes they call for.

A finding’s commit references connect its resolution to the code history. The next reviewer can inspect that history rather than accept a summary saying the problem was fixed. Checks on the normal development path use the recorded state before work is merged.

Git hooks enforce parts of that path while they are installed and configured. They are not a security boundary against an unrestricted shell. WorkBay also supports bounded work in separate working copies, with review and merge authority kept outside the worker.

Review the interface as well as the code

Interface review needs more than a code diff. I use WorkBay’s UX-map workflow to inventory an existing interface or examine a proposed change. The inventory records the screens and their regions, the states each region can show, and the actions and flows that connect them.

That inventory can be rendered as ASCII screens, Mermaid flow diagrams, and Markdown. People and AI tools can review these representations against [Heuristics Canon](/research/heuristics-canon/). The resulting findings can be added to the task record, addressed in the implementation, and checked again after the change.

The workflow separates **validation**, **rendering**, and **critique**. Validation checks whether the map has an acceptable structure. Rendering makes that structure readable in different forms. Critique asks whether particular decisions need attention; it does not implement the answers. A limited automated check pack can also flag issues such as an action pointing to a nonexistent screen.

The public WorkBay repository includes the workflow instructions. The renderer and critique implementation belong to a companion Design Canvas package outside the public mirror. The [VSW interaction reference](/research/visual-search-workbench-screen-reference/) shows how text drawings can accompany an explanation of a product.

## Separate the working tool from its evaluation

WorkBay is in use in my development practice. Its source documents how records persist, how retrieval works, and how the checks use recorded state. That establishes a working mechanism, while its effect on development effort remains a separate question.

The research follows that distinction. [Project Memory Outside the Conversation](/research/agent-memory/) explains the mechanism. [Five Questions I Ask the Project Record](/research/interrogating-agent-memory/) describes its use. [Testing Whether Project Memory Saves Work](/research/economics-of-agent-memory/) sets out the proposed evaluation.

Installation instructions and current package details are in the [WorkBay repository](https://github.com/darce/workbay).

### Apple: iPhone X Launch & Marketing Tooling
*Marketing Engineering*
Year: 2017
Tags: Front-End, CSS3 Animations, Sass, JavaScript, Node.js, Bash, Gulp, Marketing Engineering
Summary: Built launch-critical landing pages, a CSS-animated email campaign, and internal workflow tooling for Apple’s iPhone X release

## iPhone X launch pages

I worked with Apple’s marketing and design teams to build responsive landing pages for the iPhone X launch in November 2017. The work involved translating high-fidelity static comps into pixel-perfect, responsive front-end code under tight launch deadlines.
## CSS-animated email campaign

I prototyped and developed what was reportedly the marketing department’s first CSS-animated direct email campaign. The animations were designed to increase engagement without relying on JavaScript or image-heavy treatments, keeping the email lightweight and broadly compatible across clients. Internal reporting put the open rate well above the department's norm, though the sample size and the definition of an open were never recorded.
## Campaign tooling

The email production workflow was manual and repetitive, so I built a set of CLI tools in Node.js, Bash, and Gulp to automate build, preview, and deployment steps for direct email campaigns. This reduced turnaround time and made campaign production more repeatable.

### barbarabeirne.com: Archive Recovery, Rebuild & 2026 Refresh
*Artist Archive / Portfolio*
Year: 2023, 2026
Tags: Web Components, JavaScript, Sass, Rollup, Accessibility, Archive Recovery
Summary: Recovered a photography archive from a defunct Flash site, rebuilt the portfolio, and later rewrote the live site with Web Components

## The problem

Barbara Beirne's photography archive lived entirely inside a Flash website that had stopped working years ago. The original source files and developer were both unavailable. I was brought in to recover the images and rebuild the site from scratch.

## Recovering the images

The images were embedded in a compiled .SWF binary file. I used [FFDec](https://blog.free-decompiler.com/), an open-source Flash decompiler, to extract usable assets from the binary. It took some work to get clean exports, but the tool pulled the full image set.

![Black and white image of three Cambodian teens standing in front of high school lockers](/images/barbara-beirne-extracted-image.png)*Image extracted from a .SWF file using FFDec*

## The rebuild

Future compatibility was the priority, so I built the site with Web Components and Vanilla JavaScript instead of a framework that could age out. The build pipeline runs on Rollup with Sass for styling. The full-screen image carousel and all navigation are keyboard-accessible.

Barbara's images carry a lot of weight. We decided that a minimal, stark design would frame her work best.

![A group of children climbing on a large pile of debris, one waving the Ulster Banner. Image by Barbara Beirne](/images/barbara-beirne-custom-carousel-belfast-8.jpg)

## Client feedback

> "Daniel is exceptional. He was charged with recreating a photo website built initially in Flash that had long been non-functional.
Daniel came up with suggestions and solutions that were beyond what the original site had and brought it all to life.
The site is responsive and works seamlessly on all platforms and browsers.
Most importantly, Daniel is truly a pleasure to work with. He is a great communicator, delivers on time, is a perfectionist -- in the best sense of the word - and is thoughtful and considerate.
I had no references to go by when we hired Daniel and couldn't be more pleased with his work."
>> *Alison Cornyn*

>> *Artist + Co-Founder and Creative Director Picture Projects*

>> *June 13, 2023*

### bauhausdances.org: Visual Identity & Custom WordPress Theme
*Arts & Film (Independent)*
Year: 2023
Tags: WordPress, Custom Theme, PHP, CSS Animation, JavaScript, Video, Accessibility
Summary: Designed a visual identity rooted in the film’s source material and built a custom WordPress theme with self-hosted video

## The design challenge

Filmmaker Debra McCall wanted a new website for her 1982 film recreating Oskar Schlemmer’s Bauhaus Dances. The challenge was to reflect Bauhaus visual language without falling into generic arts-site conventions.

The visual direction grew out of the film’s Hoop Dance sequence, where white rings create stark geometric forms against a dark stage. I used that imagery as the basis for the site’s visual system and interaction language.

![Reinfentanz performance. A dancer stands on one foot with her left foot stretched back, holding five white rings. Two rings form concentric circles near her head, three form concentric circles below her hips.](/images/bauhaus-dances-hoop-dance.jpg)

A subtle ring-based interaction, derived from the Hoop Dance imagery, adds motion without overpowering the content.

## Implementation

I built a custom WordPress theme on top of [Underscores](https://underscores.me/) so the client could manage content independently. The site also uses self-hosted video with caching optimizations to keep load times low without relying on third-party embeds.

## Research

### Finding a Visual Direction with UMAP
*How similarity search becomes a way to explore a photo collection*
Tags: Visual Search, UMAP, Interaction Design, On-Device ML, Research
Summary: How Visual Search Workbench connects search, a UMAP map, and an image grid to help people explore a photo collection and develop a visual direction.

A useful picture can change what you are looking for. You may start with a subject in mind, then notice a colour relationship or composition worth following. That shift interests me because it turns search into part of developing an idea.

[Visual Search Workbench](/projects/visual-search-workbench/) gives that shift a path through a photo collection. A search produces candidates; a candidate can become the next query. Alongside the search, a UMAP map offers regions of related images to explore.

The design brings together **search**, a **map**, and an **image grid**. Search finds a starting point. The map offers a view of relationships beyond a ranked list. The image grid makes a selected region available for judgment.

```text
Photo folders you choose
          │
      Search index
          │
  Words or reference image
          │
    Candidate photographs
       [A] [B] [C]
       [D] [E] [F]
```

_Interaction schematic: chosen folders supply an index. Either a text query or a reference image leads to a grid of candidate photographs._

![The Similarity map in Visual Search Workbench, with photographs from a selected region available in the grid.](/images/work/sis-layers-umap.png)

*Application capture from version 0.2.0. The companion interaction reference draws on the 0.2.3 product record.*

## Search can lead somewhere you did not expect

Search often starts with a fairly definite task: find a photograph you remember. A description can bring likely candidates into view even when you have forgotten the filename. Once you recognise the picture, the search has done its job.

Visual exploration has a less definite endpoint. A photograph can be useful because it suggests what to look for next. In a reference collection, for example, you might follow a visual resemblance toward a composition you had not yet formulated. The value of that next image depends on the idea you are developing, not only on its match to the original words.

VSW lets a result become the next query through **Find similar**. The chosen image becomes the reference for a new ranking, with its name visible above the results. **Back to text results** provides a return to the earlier search. These controls make it possible to follow an image without treating every query as an unrelated start.

```text
Text query ► [A] [B] [C] [D]
                    │
               Find similar
                    │
              B is the reference
                    │
                [E] [F] [G]
                    │
             Back to text results
```

_Interaction schematic: a text query returns candidate photographs; choosing photograph B as a reference opens a new similarity search, with a return path to the text results._

![A photograph used as a Find similar reference, with the reference named and a return to text results available.](/images/work/sis-similarity-search.png)

## The map makes related images browsable

A ranked list arranges candidates around one query. A map provides a different way to look through the material: inspect a region, see which pictures it contains, and choose where to go next. UMAP supplies the arrangement for VSW’s Similarity view.

### How UMAP works, in plain terms

The app’s image model turns each photograph into an **embedding**, a list of numbers used to compare images. Those numbers work together as a representation; individual entries are not labels such as “red,” “flower,” or “portrait.” Comparing the representations gives the software a way to find nearby images without consulting manually assigned tags.

Those nearby images form **neighbourhoods**. UMAP represents neighbourhood relationships as a weighted graph: a network of connections whose strengths reflect the local relationships in the input. It then looks for a lower-dimensional arrangement that preserves those relationships as well as possible. This is the graph-and-layout process described in the [UMAP authors’ explanation](https://umap-learn.readthedocs.io/en/latest/how_umap_works.html).

The arrangement becomes the map on screen. Its purpose is to make some of those relationships available to explore while accepting that a compact layout loses information. The image model supplies the representations; UMAP arranges them; the person decides which pictures are worth following.

### What the arrangement means

A neighbourhood is a place to investigate, not a category the app has established. Its pictures may be useful together, or their resemblance may be unimportant to the current brief. The photographs themselves let you make that distinction.

The layout also changes how relationships look. A wide gap between groups is not an exact measure of their difference, and a dense patch does not establish the density of the original representations. Apparent splits can arise during the reduction, as the [UMAP clustering guide](https://umap-learn.readthedocs.io/en/latest/clustering.html) explains.

Two settings help explain why maps can look different: **neighbourhood size** and **minimum distance**. Neighbourhood size determines how broadly the method looks around each item, shifting emphasis between fine local detail and a wider arrangement. Minimum distance affects how tightly points can pack in the layout. The [parameter guide](https://umap-learn.readthedocs.io/en/latest/parameters.html) illustrates both effects. These are explanations of the method, not controls I am claiming the current app exposes.

## The image grid makes the map usable

A region on the map becomes an image selection. That selection appears in the grid, where you can inspect the photographs at a useful size. A promising photograph can then supply the reference for another search.

This connection gives the map a role in the interaction. The map helps you choose where to look; the grid shows what is there. Without the grid, a point cloud would reveal an arrangement but provide little basis for deciding whether the pictures suit your work.

```text
Similarity overview
┌───────────────────────────┐
│   . .              . .    │
│  ┌─────────┐              │
│  │ A  B  C │      . .     │
│  └─────────┘              │
│       . .                 │
└───────────────────────────┘
       Selected region
              │
              ▾
      Linked image grid
      ┌───────────────────┐
      │ [A]  [B]  [C]     │
      │ Inspect these     │
      │ photographs       │
      └───────────────────┘
```

_Conceptual map-to-grid relationship, not a reconstruction of the application: selecting a region containing photographs A, B, and C shows those same photographs in the linked grid. Other regions remain outside the selection._

The grid and map also need distinct interpretations. A search ranking compares the query with the image representations. The distance between marks on the displayed map is not that ranking. Keeping those roles clear lets the map support browsing without asking it to be a precise measuring instrument.

## Keep the exploration on an everyday Mac

Local processing was a design constraint for the app. The photographs stay in the folders the person chooses, and the models ship with the application. I tested that arrangement on an 8 GB Apple Silicon Mac.

That constraint extends beyond running the model. A selected region must also deliver photographs that can be inspected. Release 0.2.3 addressed thumbnail retries, a change recorded in the [release repository](https://github.com/darce/visual-search-workbench). The 8 GB test identifies a working configuration; larger-library performance and peak memory still need measurement.

## Test retrieval and exploration separately

The design now has an implementation to evaluate. I use screen inventories and the running app to check the relationship between a query, a selection, and the next action. The [interaction reference](/research/visual-search-workbench-screen-reference/) records that relationship. WorkBay and the [Heuristics Canon](/research/heuristics-canon/) support these reviews, but outside-user evaluation remains to be done.

That evaluation needs to distinguish **retrieval** from **exploration**. Retrieval asks whether someone can find a remembered photograph. Exploration asks whether someone can assemble useful references for a creative brief, including pictures that change the direction of the brief.

For retrieval, I would examine completion, mistakes, and effort. For exploration, I would examine the images people keep, the paths they take, and their reasons for continuing from one picture to another. Comparing the map with the grid and image-to-image search would help establish what the map contributes.

The question is whether visual navigation helps someone develop an idea. A surprising selection may be useful even when it takes them beyond the subject they first searched for.

### Visual Search Workbench: Search and Exploration
*Follow a query into similar images, a map selection, and further exploration*
Tags: Visual Search, UMAP, Interaction Design, Interface Reference
Summary: An interaction reference for Visual Search Workbench: begin with words or a picture, follow similar images, and inspect a UMAP map selection in the image grid.

This reference follows a path through [Visual Search Workbench](/projects/visual-search-workbench/): give the search a starting point, make a promising picture the next query, then explore related material on the Similarity map. The selected images remain available in the grid for inspection and further use.

The application captures are the existing 0.2.0 screenshots; the descriptions draw on the 0.2.3 product record. **The text drawings are explanatory schematics, not screenshots, exact layouts, or newly verified interface strings.** Letters stand for photographs rather than measured search results.

## 1. Give the search a starting point

The search uses an index of the folders you choose. The index lets the app compare their photographs while the originals remain in place. It accepts a text query or a reference image, with neither route requiring advance tagging.

A text query is useful when you can describe what you want. A reference image is useful when showing an example is easier. Both routes lead to candidates that you can inspect in the image grid.

```text
Photo folders you choose
          │
      Search index
          │
  Words or reference image
          │
    Candidate photographs
       [A] [B] [C]
       [D] [E] [F]
```

_Interaction schematic: chosen folders supply an index. Either a text query or a reference image leads to a grid of candidate photographs._

## 2. Make a result the next query

A selected photograph opens for inspection. **Find similar** makes that photograph the reference for another search. The new view names the reference and offers **Back to text results**, keeping the change of query visible.

![Find similar results with a flower photograph identified as the reference image.](/images/work/sis-similarity-search.png)

```text
Text query ► [A] [B] [C] [D]
                    │
               Find similar
                    │
              B is the reference
                    │
                [E] [F] [G]
                    │
             Back to text results
```

_Interaction schematic: a text query returns candidate photographs; choosing photograph B as a reference opens a new similarity search, with a return path to the text results._

The result has become a direction through the collection. Following it can bring useful material into view even when that material was difficult to describe in the first query.

## 3. Explore a region on the Similarity map

The **Similarity** view offers a spatial arrangement of related images. That arrangement is built with UMAP, which takes numerical image representations, identifies their neighbourhood relationships, and looks for a layout that preserves those relationships in fewer dimensions.

In practical terms, UMAP turns many-number comparisons into places to browse on a screen. Those places are suggestions for exploration, not automatically named categories. The [design article](/research/visual-search-workbench-process/) explains the method and how it differs from search ranking.

![The Similarity view and the photographs associated with a selected region.](/images/work/sis-layers-umap.png)

A selected region becomes a set of photographs in the linked grid. The grid lets you inspect the images behind the marks and choose whether any is worth following.

```text
Similarity overview
┌───────────────────────────┐
│   . .              . .    │
│  ┌─────────┐              │
│  │ A  B  C │      . .     │
│  └─────────┘              │
│       . .                 │
└───────────────────────────┘
       Selected region
              │
              ▾
      Linked image grid
      ┌───────────────────┐
      │ [A]  [B]  [C]     │
      │ Inspect these     │
      │ photographs       │
      └───────────────────┘
```

_Conceptual map-to-grid relationship, not a reconstruction of the application: selecting a region containing photographs A, B, and C shows those same photographs in the linked grid. Other regions remain outside the selection._

Nearby marks suggest material to inspect. Their spacing is not an exact measure of how different the photographs are. Judging the photographs in the grid is what gives the map selection a purpose.

## 4. Examine the selection by place or time

The selected material can be examined through **Similarity**, **Places**, and **Timeline**. Each view organises the collection using different information.

| View | Basis of the view |
| --- | --- |
| Similarity | Relationships between numerical image representations. |
| Places | Recorded coordinates, explored geographically. |
| Timeline | Dates, explored across broader or narrower periods. |

Selection carries between the views, and each view retains its zoom and pan when you change tabs. The views therefore offer different routes through related material without requiring you to rebuild the view each time.

A place-based selection can also include photographs outside the current text results. Those photographs are listed without a search rank, keeping the geographic selection distinct from the query’s ranking.

## 5. Inspect a photograph or use a cutout

An individual photograph can be inspected with its available file metadata. It can also supply a subject for the experimental cutout workflow, which proposes layers with transparent backgrounds.

![A cat image with experimental cutout layers available for inspection.](/images/work/sis-cat-layers-detail.png)

The proposed layers can be inspected and saved for use elsewhere. A recognisable subject does not guarantee a usable separation or edge, so the cutout still needs checking. This remains a secondary workflow alongside search and exploration.

## Use the reference to review the interaction

This sequence connects a query to a result, a result to another query, and a map region to the images it contains. I use representations like these to examine whether the next action follows clearly from the current selection.

A structured UX map can provide an interface inventory and render it as text screens for human and AI review. The running interface still needs to be checked for behaviour and visual quality. The schematics on this page are selective explanations; they are not claimed as generated UX-map output or as drawings checked by the product’s source-string tests.

Read [Finding a Visual Direction with UMAP](/research/visual-search-workbench-process/) for the design idea, or return to the [product page](/projects/visual-search-workbench/) for installation and release status.

### Project Memory Outside the Conversation
*The record, retrieval layer, and context packet behind WorkBay*
Tags: Agent Workflows, SQLite, Semantic Retrieval, Research
Summary: WorkBay separates the stored project record from the retrieval layer that finds it and the context packet a coding session reads.

A later coding session needs more than an account of what happened. It may need the reason an approach was rejected, the finding that remains unresolved, or the test result behind a completion claim. [WorkBay](/projects/workbay/) keeps that material in a project record outside the conversation.

The design has three parts: a **record**, a **retrieval layer**, and a **context packet**. The record preserves decisions and evidence. The retrieval layer finds material that may matter to the current task. The context packet gives the next session a selected portion to read.

These parts describe the mechanism. [The field note](/research/interrogating-agent-memory/) describes how I use it, and [the evaluation proposal](/research/economics-of-agent-memory/) asks whether it reduces work at comparable quality.

## The record preserves decisions and evidence

Each WorkBay repository has a SQLite file at `.task-state/handoff.db`. SQLite stores the database locally without requiring a separate database server. The database contains tasks, decisions, review findings, blockers, and test records.

Those records keep different aspects of the work distinct. A decision has a rationale. A finding has a status and a recorded resolution. A test has a command and result, with task and commit information helping connect the evidence to the work it concerns.

A later session can therefore retrieve a decision as a decision. It need not reconstruct the rationale from a recap saying that planning was completed. The rationale still needs to be checked against present requirements, but the earlier reasoning is available for that check.

## The retrieval layer finds material in the record

Retrieval depends on what the session already knows. A known task or finding can be looked up directly. Known wording can be found through full-text search. A question phrased differently from the earlier record can use optional semantic retrieval.

Semantic retrieval compares numerical representations called **embeddings**. An embedding represents a piece of text as a list of numbers. Comparing these representations can bring related records into view even when their wording differs.

A retrieved record might contain the rationale for an approach rejected earlier. That rationale can explain the original constraint; the constraint can then be compared with the current implementation. The result is a reason to examine the earlier decision, not an instruction to repeat it.

### Keep the index tied to the record

The embeddings form an index over selected fields in the database. Links and text fingerprints connect the index entries to their source records. Those records remain available independently of the index, so the index can be rebuilt without becoming the authoritative version of a decision.

The related-prior-work tool returns candidates for a human or agent to read. Its contract prevents those candidates from automatically closing findings or becoming inputs to a merge decision. Similarity can change which record looks worth inspecting; it cannot establish that two findings are duplicates or that either has been fixed.

The tool also reports why a lookup returns nothing. An empty store, an unavailable provider, incompatible model information, and no result above the threshold are distinct outcomes. In particular, no result above the threshold does not prove the relevant history is absent. The [retrieval implementation](https://github.com/darce/workbay/blob/main/packages/mcp-workbay-handoff/src/workbay_handoff_mcp/embeddings/related_prior_work.py) documents these boundaries.

## The context packet gives the session a selection

A context packet brings selected records into the current conversation. The packet must be bounded because the conversation still has finite space. Loading every past record would compete with the task the session is meant to complete.

The choice of records therefore matters. In an earlier audit of my repositories, review findings accounted for roughly four fifths of embedded entries, with decision rationales making up most of the remainder. That historical distribution describes the material available to retrieve; it is not a target for every project.

The useful question is whether a selected record changes the next decision. A paragraph can sound relevant without supplying the constraint or unresolved finding the session actually needs. That difference between apparent relevance and useful context is one reason retrieval needs evaluation.

## Portability follows the record

The structured record can be exported and read by different supported coding tools. A session in a new tool can retrieve history written by another tool without having its entire conversation. The new tool still needs its own authentication and setup, and its capabilities may differ.

The database stays out of version control by default because it can contain sensitive project material. Keeping the file local does not make every use of its contents private: a context packet sent to a hosted model sends that selected material to the provider. Export and model use both require attention to what the record contains.

## Test what the record changes

The implementation makes recorded history persistent and retrievable. It cannot preserve reasoning that was never recorded or guarantee that each useful record will be found.

Those limits define an evaluation question: when a session receives selected history, does it complete comparable work with less effort? The [economics article](/research/economics-of-agent-memory/) separates the cost of supplying that history from its effect on the result.

### Five Questions I Ask the Project Record
*Look for recurring trouble, earlier fixes, decision reasons, completion evidence, and failed approaches*
Tags: Agent Workflows, Project Memory, Field Notes
Summary: Five recurring questions show how I use WorkBay’s project record to examine an earlier decision before making the next one.

I use the project record when the next coding decision depends on work outside the current conversation. The record can bring back an earlier rationale or show that a new-looking failure has already occurred across several tasks.

Five questions recur in my use of [WorkBay](/projects/workbay/): **where trouble repeats**, **whether a fix exists**, **why an approach was chosen**, **what supports completion**, and **what has already failed**. Each question calls for a different part of the record.

The examples below are field observations from my development practice, not a controlled productivity study. [Project Memory Outside the Conversation](/research/agent-memory/) explains the storage and retrieval mechanism.

## Where does trouble repeat?

A review usually concerns the work in front of it. A sequence of reviews can reveal trouble that keeps returning across tasks. The project record makes that sequence available even when no single session has seen all of it.

In one earlier audit, roughly three quarters of the recorded reviews in a small project had failed. That pattern prompted a closer look at the architecture. The count did not establish the cause: task selection and review practice could also have affected the proportion.

The coral cluster illustrates what the wider view makes visible: repeated failures that a single session might miss. The findings behind the count were the material to inspect. Their shared constraints could suggest a broader problem, while differences between them could show that the apparent pattern had several causes. The count directed the investigation; the findings had to support the diagnosis.

## Does a useful fix already exist?

A new finding may resemble a problem recorded under different wording. Semantic retrieval can surface an earlier resolution, which a human or agent can compare with the current code.

The resolution may contain more than a patch. It can preserve the constraint that made the patch necessary or the reason a simpler change failed. That explanation helps determine whether the earlier fix applies now.

An earlier fix remains a candidate until its conditions and recorded status have been checked. Copying the patch without that check would replace repeated investigation with a different risk: applying the right answer to the wrong problem.

## Why was this approach chosen?

A decision record preserves the reasons behind a choice. Those reasons give a later discussion a starting point even when the people or tools involved were absent from the original conversation.

For example, a later session may question why a site uses static output rather than server rendering. The recorded rationale can identify the requirements the choice addressed. Those requirements can then be compared with the needs of the current work.

A changed requirement may justify a changed decision. The record should make that change deliberate, not keep the original choice closed forever. Its value is distinguishing a new reason from an old debate whose reasoning has been forgotten.

## What supports the completion claim?

A completion claim needs evidence tied to the work being assessed. WorkBay can preserve review verdicts and test records alongside task and commit information. That information lets another reviewer inspect which commands ran, what they returned, and which revision they concern.

The revision matters because a test result from earlier code does not automatically establish the state of the current code. A useful review follows the evidence back to the change instead of relying on a summary saying that the task passed.

Another model can perform that review without inheriting the author’s conversation. Semantic search may help locate the relevant discussion, but the completion assessment depends on the exact records and the code.

## What has already failed?

A failed approach leaves information that can disappear from a recap of the eventual success. Blockers and abandoned attempts preserve that information, including why the approach was set aside.

The reason distinguishes an option that was temporarily unavailable from one that produced incorrect results. An unavailable dependency may later become usable. An incorrect result may expose a constraint that still applies.

The history therefore does not forbid another attempt. It makes the next attempt answer a specific question: what has changed since this failed?

## From a useful lookup to an evaluated benefit

These questions give the record a practical role in the next decision. The examples show what can be inspected; they do not establish how often retrieval finds the right material or how much work it saves.

That benefit needs a comparison that measures both effort and the resulting work. [Testing Whether Project Memory Saves Work](/research/economics-of-agent-memory/) sets out the proposed comparison, keeping the evaluation separate from these observations of use.

### Testing Whether Project Memory Saves Work
*What an audit shows, what a comparison must test, and what would count as a useful result*
Tags: Agent Workflows, Evaluation, Token Use, Research
Summary: An audit snapshot describes WorkBay context packets. A proposed paired comparison tests whether they reduce task token use without lowering quality.

Project history is worth supplying to a coding session when it helps the session complete the task. It may prevent a repeated investigation or bring an important constraint back into view. It may also distract the agent or revive a decision that no longer applies.

This proposed WorkBay evaluation asks whether a task-relevant context packet reduces total token use **without lowering outcome quality**. Fewer tokens alone would not establish a useful result if the agent completed less of the task or introduced more errors.

The argument has three parts: **the audit snapshot**, **the comparison**, and **the decision criterion**. The audit snapshot describes the recorded cost and contents. The comparison tests whether supplying the history changes the work. The decision criterion specifies what result would justify a savings claim. No controlled-trial result is reported here.

## The audit snapshot describes cost and contents

An earlier audit examined three project `handoff.db` databases. Its summary reported small initial context packets alongside much larger recorded task totals. It also found that most findings marked resolved had a written resolution.

| Audit observation | What it describes |
| --- | --- |
| About 300 tokens in the average compact packet | The recorded size of an initial selection of project history. |
| A median recorded task near three hundred thousand tokens | Task-level totals, rather than the cost of one model request. |
| Recorded tasks ranging from a few thousand to hundreds of millions of tokens | A heterogeneous workload, including very large tasks split across worker lanes. |
| About 99% of resolved findings carrying a written resolution; no audited codebase below 97% | Whether a resolution was recorded, not whether another task would benefit from it. |

These figures are descriptive aggregates from that audit. The summary does not provide the underlying rows or per-measure sample sizes, so the figures should not be treated as a general performance benchmark.

The three steps between the packet and median-task markers show a difference of roughly a thousandfold. The packet’s recorded size is small relative to those task totals. That comparison concerns the amount of text supplied at the start, not the complete cost of remembering. Retrieval, later context use, and decisions made from stale material may add costs elsewhere. A token count is also not itself a monetary return.

### The audit cannot establish an effect

The audit’s main limitation is an instrumentation mismatch. Interactive sessions received context packets but lacked the audited task-level token measurement used in the analysis. Orchestrated worker lanes supplied token measurements but did not receive those packets.

That mismatch prevents a meaningful treated-versus-untreated comparison. The two groups differ in their work and measurement as well as their use of project history. A controlled comparison must record both the intervention and its cost for the same assigned tasks.

The resolution figures have a similar boundary. A written resolution establishes that material exists to retrieve. It does not establish that retrieval selects the right resolution, or that an agent uses it well. Those effects belong in the comparison.

## The comparison tests whether the packet changes the work

The proposed comparison runs each selected task twice from the same base commit: once with a frozen, task-relevant packet and once without that packet. Both runs receive the same task specification, model configuration, and resource limits. Their order is randomised, and neither updates shared memory until the pair is complete.

The comparison needs **calibration**, a **content probe**, and **matched task pairs**. Each stage answers a different question before the savings claim is assessed.

**Calibration** uses A/A pairs: two cold runs with the same starting conditions. The variation between those attempts estimates how much results can differ without the memory intervention. That variation informs the sample-size procedure for the main comparison.

**The content probe** compares a relevant packet with an equally sized unrelated packet. This tests whether relevant content makes a difference beyond merely adding text. A relevant-versus-unrelated result would not, by itself, establish a benefit over receiving no packet.

**Matched task pairs** provide that final comparison. Each pair contains one run with the relevant packet and one without it. A reviewer who does not know which condition produced the work scores both results against a fixed rubric. The system records total tokens per assigned task, including unsuccessful attempts.

Keeping unsuccessful attempts in the analysis matters because a quick failure can use fewer tokens than a completed task. The quality assessment and failure rate must therefore accompany the token result.

## The decision criterion includes quality

The existing proposal sets a target of at least a **20% reduction in token use**, while keeping blinded quality within an acceptable margin declared before the trial. The target is a decision criterion, not a prediction.

The readout should report the paired effect with an uncertainty interval, alongside the quality comparison and failure rate. A reduction in tokens would qualify only if the quality condition also holds. An inconclusive interval would remain inconclusive rather than being presented as a savings result.

The initial comparison would concern one repository’s workload. A result there would not establish the same effect for other projects, models, or teams without further evaluation.

## Specify the measurement before running it

The protocol still needs its operational definitions completed. The interactive task meter and packet-selection rule must be recorded and frozen. The quality rubric, acceptable quality margin, and sample-size procedure must be specified before the main comparison.

Those definitions determine what the result will mean. Changing them after inspecting the results could change which runs count as successful or which apparent saving meets the target. Fixing them first makes the eventual decision checkable.

This is a proposed evaluation, not a completed or externally registered study. The Canon’s [UXR-01](https://github.com/darce/heuristics-canon/blob/main/lexicons/interaction-ux.md#uxr-01) and [EXP-01](https://github.com/darce/heuristics-canon/blob/main/lexicons/epistemics.md#exp-01) supply relevant checks: measure at the level of the claim and use a controlled comparison for the claimed effect.

## The decision in the meantime

I use WorkBay to retain inspectable project history and resume work across coding sessions. Those capabilities can be examined in the implementation. Whether supplying selected history also reduces total work at comparable quality remains open until the comparison is run.

[Project Memory Outside the Conversation](/research/agent-memory/) describes that implementation. [Five Questions I Ask the Project Record](/research/interrogating-agent-memory/) describes how I use it in practice.

### Heuristics Canon
*Connect a review finding to a reason for changing the work*
Tags: Design Review, Engineering, Writing, Research
Summary: Heuristics Canon gives design, engineering, and writing reviews specific triggers and questions, with references that let another reviewer examine the reasoning.

A review becomes useful when its finding is specific enough to examine. “Improve the navigation” leaves the problem open to interpretation. A finding that identifies two conflicting destinations gives the designer something to inspect and a decision to make.

Heuristics Canon is a collection I maintain to support that kind of critique in design, engineering, and writing. I use it with people and AI tools to connect an observed issue to a reason for changing it. A cited rule makes that reason available to challenge as well as to apply.

## Make the rule inspectable

A Canon rule has an observable **trigger**, a proposed **action**, and a **question** that tests whether it applies. The trigger identifies a situation in the artifact under review. The action suggests what to do about it. The question helps the reviewer decide whether the situation actually warrants that response.

A stable ID identifies the rule, and a source reference records its basis. Those references let another reviewer follow the reasoning without relying on the first reviewer’s explanation alone. Where the basis is provisional or unsourced practice, the collection marks that distinction.

The rules are grouped into lexicons, including interaction design, accessibility, engineering, and writing. These are parts of the same review practice: an interface decision may depend on implementation constraints, while a claim about that interface may need a different kind of evidence. A review retrieves the relevant rules rather than applying the whole collection as a checklist.

## Review a map and the images it represents

Visual Search Workbench connects a Similarity map with an image grid. Reviewing that connection raises two separate questions: **does the selection remain recognisable across the views**, and **does the explanation describe the map accurately**?

**The selection** is a coordination problem. Selecting a region on the map should leave the same material recognisable in the grid, where the photographs can be inspected. The Canon records that principle as [VIZ-15](https://github.com/darce/heuristics-canon/blob/main/lexicons/interaction-ux.md#viz-15).

**The explanation** is an interpretation problem. Wording that presents a gap between UMAP groups as an exact measure of visual difference would claim more than the layout supports. [VIZ-18](https://github.com/darce/heuristics-canon/blob/main/lexicons/interaction-ux.md#viz-18) supplies a check on that inference.

These examples show how a rule can focus a critique. They do not establish that the map helps people explore a collection. The [VSW design article](/research/visual-search-workbench-process/) treats that as a separate evaluation question.

## Carry the finding into the work

My workflow combines the Canon with [WorkBay](/projects/workbay/). An interface can be inventoried in a UX map and rendered as text screens or flow diagrams. A reviewer examines those representations and records a finding with the rule and artifact it concerns.

The finding can then be stored against the task. A change addresses it, and a later review checks the result. Keeping the finding available allows the reviewer to ask whether the change resolved the original issue instead of relying on a broad statement that the interface was improved.

The running interface remains part of that review. A map can expose an action or flow, but it does not reproduce the entire visual and interactive experience.

## Question the finding before changing the product

A critique can be wrong even when it cites a rule. The finding itself needs scrutiny before it justifies a change.

In an earlier review from my practice, an agent proposed changing roughly forty code sites it had classified as defective. Checking that classification first found that about a third were false positives, and the proposed sweep narrowed. This is a field example of testing a finding, not an accuracy measurement for the Canon.

Another recorded correction concerned a failure described as present in shipped work. The failure existed only in a constructed test input, so the claim had to be narrowed before it could justify a production change. In both cases, examining the basis of the finding changed the proposed work.

## Keep the source and version with the reasoning

A source reference establishes where a rule came from. It does not establish that the rule applies to every artifact or that a product has passed user validation. The trigger and any relevant exception still require judgment.

The writing lexicon makes this boundary explicit: some rules are provisional editorial checks, not proof of AI authorship. Repeating a topic can help a reader follow an explanation, for example; repetition alone does not establish that the prose should be changed. The effect on the passage matters.

A review also needs the version of the rule it used. An ID can remain stable while the wording or source changes. The [consumer guide](https://github.com/darce/heuristics-canon/blob/main/AGENTS.md) describes version and digest checks so the basis of an earlier critique can be recovered.

## Measure review quality, not the number of citations

The field examples show findings leading to revisions or being withdrawn. They do not establish that the full collection improves review outcomes compared with a smaller checklist or another reviewer.

A comparison would need to examine consequential findings, missed defects, false positives, and reviewer effort on comparable artifacts. Those measures concern the quality of the review. The number of rule IDs cited concerns only its activity.

The [public repository](https://github.com/darce/heuristics-canon) contains the rules, source references, and longer reasoning cards for decisions that need more context.

### 3D Without Canvas or WebGL
*Rotation matrices with DOM Elements & CSS transforms; no Canvas or WebGL*
Tags: Linear Algebra, 3D Graphics, TypeScript, DOM Manipulation, CSS Transforms
Summary: A browser experiment that makes rotation matrices and perspective projection, normally abstracted by WebGL, visible using only TypeScript, DOM elements, and CSS transforms

> **What this is:** a small experiment showing how 3D rotation and projection map to browser rendering using only DOM elements, TypeScript, and CSS transforms.
> **What this is not:** a general-purpose 3D engine or a recommended production rendering pipeline.

## Why DOM Instead of Canvas?

In this experiment, the cube is not drawn on a canvas. Each vertex is a `div` element, positioned using CSS transforms.

This is a deliberate constraint: no canvas, no WebGL, no engine; just enough code to make the math visible from matrix multiplication to motion on screen.
## The Problem

A cube has eight vertices. Each vertex is a point in space: $(x, y, z)$.

To rotate the cube, we need new coordinates for every vertex—coordinates that place each point in its rotated position.

Rotation matrices perform that transformation. In this demo, the math is done directly in TypeScript and the result is pushed into CSS transforms.

## One Axis at a Time

Rotation around an axis leaves that axis unchanged. Rotating around $z$ moves points in the $xy$-plane. Rotating around $x$ moves points in the $yz$-plane.

Each axis has its own matrix. In the plane perpendicular to that axis the picture is a 2D rotation: counterclockwise when $y$ points up (the math convention), clockwise when $y$ points down (the screen).

### Around X

The first row is $[1, 0, 0]$. This preserves $x$:

$$R_x(\theta) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ 0 & \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}$$

```typescript
const rotationX = (vertexArray: Vertex[], angle: number): Vertex[] => {
    const rotationMatrix = [
        [1, 0, 0],
        [0, Math.cos(angle), -Math.sin(angle)],
        [0, Math.sin(angle), Math.cos(angle)]
    ]
    return transformPointsWithMatrix(vertexArray, rotationMatrix)
}
```

### Around Y

The middle row is $[0, 1, 0]$. No rotation around the $y$-axis leaves $y$ unchanged while rotating points in the $xz$-plane:

$$R_y(\theta) = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & 0 & \sin\theta \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -\sin\theta & 0 & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}$$
```typescript
const rotationY = (vertexArray: Vertex[], angle: number): Vertex[] => {
    const rotationMatrix = [
        [Math.cos(angle), 0, Math.sin(angle)],
        [0, 1, 0],
        [-Math.sin(angle), 0, Math.cos(angle)]
    ]
    return transformPointsWithMatrix(vertexArray, rotationMatrix)
}
```

### Around Z

The last row is $[0, 0, 1]$. This preserves $z$:

$$R_z(\theta) = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta & 0 \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

```typescript
const rotationZ = (vertexArray: Vertex[], angle: number): Vertex[] => {
    const rotationMatrix = [
        [Math.cos(angle), -Math.sin(angle), 0],
        [Math.sin(angle), Math.cos(angle), 0],
        [0, 0, 1]
    ]
    return transformPointsWithMatrix(vertexArray, rotationMatrix)
}
```

## Applying a Rotation

To rotate a vertex, multiply the matrix by its coordinates:

$$\begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ z' \end{bmatrix} = R \cdot \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix}$$

The result $(x', y', z')$ is the rotated position. Do that for every vertex and the whole shape turns. The origin stays put.

In this demo, that math is done in plain TypeScript:
```typescript
const matrixMultiplyVertex = (matrix: number[][], vertex: Vertex): Vertex => {
    const result: number[][] = []
    for (let i = 0; i < matrix.length; i++) {
        let sum = 0
        sum += matrix[i][0] * vertex.x
        sum += matrix[i][1] * vertex.y
        sum += matrix[i][2] * vertex.z
```
